claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength.
The low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi arise from high dislocation mobility.
High dislocation mobility enables rapid dynamic recovery during deformation.
Dynamic recovery in this alloy includes dislocation cross-slip and annihilation.
Rapid dynamic recovery prevents dislocation pile-up and accumulation.
Reduced dislocation accumulation suppresses strain hardening.
Suppressed strain hardening explains the alloy's relatively low hardness and strength despite its ductility.
The starting material is equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a homogenized, single-phase solid-solution state.
The starting material has inherent ductility.
Dislocation density and substructure evolution are the proposed structural mediators of the mechanical response.
At higher strain rates, the alloy will exhibit lower-than-expected dislocation entanglement.
At higher strain rates, the alloy will develop well-defined dislocation-cell structures indicative of dynamic recovery.
At higher strain rates, observations will show signs of dislocation annihilation.
The alloy will have lower strain-hardening coefficients than conventional FCC metals in which dislocation pile-up is more pronounced.
The proposed mechanism applies at room temperature under uniaxial compression in the elastic-plastic regime over strain rates from 10^-4 to 10^2 s^-1.
A controlled strain-rate series combined with in situ TEM or synchrotron X-ray diffraction can track dislocation evolution while stress-strain curves quantify strain hardening.
Observation of substantial dislocation pile-up, high dislocation density, and robust strain hardening would falsify rapid dynamic recovery as the primary strength-limiting mechanism.
